claim: Coronavirus disease-19 (COVID-19) causes immune perturbations which may persist long term.
source: Coronavirus disease-19 (COVID-19) causes immune perturbations which may persist long term, and patients frequently report ongoing symptoms for months after recovery.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about COVID-19's effects.

claim: Patients frequently report ongoing symptoms for months after COVID-19 recovery.
source: Coronavirus disease-19 (COVID-19) causes immune perturbations which may persist long term, and patients frequently report ongoing symptoms for months after recovery.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about COVID-19 patients.

claim: At 3 months post-admission, patients with severe disease displayed persistent activation of CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells based on expression of HLA-DR, CD38, Ki67, and granzyme B.
source: At 3 months, patients with severe disease displayed persistent activation of CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells, based on expression of HLA-DR, CD38, Ki67, and granzyme B, and elevated plasma levels of interleukin-4 (IL-4), IL-7, IL-17, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) compared to mild and/or moderate patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in the manuscript showing increased expression of these markers in severe patients.

claim: At 3 months post-admission, patients with severe disease had elevated plasma levels of IL-4, IL-7, IL-17, and TNF-α compared to mild and/or moderate patients.
source: At 3 months, patients with severe disease displayed persistent activation of CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells, based on expression of HLA-DR, CD38, Ki67, and granzyme B, and elevated plasma levels of interleukin-4 (IL-4), IL-7, IL-17, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) compared to mild and/or moderate patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by Luminex cytokine measurements presented in Figure 3.

claim: Plasma from severe patients at 3 months caused T-cells from healthy donors to upregulate IL-15Rα.
source: Plasma from severe patients at 3 months caused T-cells from healthy donors to upregulate IL-15Rα, suggesting that plasma factors in severe patients may increase T-cell responsiveness to IL-15-driven bystander activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-culture experiments shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Plasma factors in severe patients may increase T-cell responsiveness to IL-15-driven bystander activation.
source: Plasma from severe patients at 3 months caused T-cells from healthy donors to upregulate IL-15Rα, suggesting that plasma factors in severe patients may increase T-cell responsiveness to IL-15-driven bystander activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the IL-15Rα upregulation data.

claim: Patients with severe disease reported a higher number of long COVID symptoms.
source: Patients with severe disease reported a higher number of long COVID symptoms which did not however correlate with cellular immune activation/pro-inflammatory cytokines after adjusting for age, sex, and disease severity.
evidence: This is supported by symptom data presented in Table 1 and Figure 6.

claim: Long COVID symptoms did not correlate with cellular immune activation/pro-inflammatory cytokines after adjusting for age, sex, and disease severity.
source: Patients with severe disease reported a higher number of long COVID symptoms which did not however correlate with cellular immune activation/pro-inflammatory cytokines after adjusting for age, sex, and disease severity.
evidence: This is based on Poisson regression analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Long COVID and persistent immune activation may correlate independently with severe disease.
source: Our data suggests that long COVID and persistent immune activation may correlate independently with severe disease.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the statistical analyses.

claim: Acute COVID-19 causes a profound activation of innate and adaptive immune cells.
source: There is evidence showing that acute COVID-19 causes a profound activation of innate and adaptive immune cells, and distinct immunological signatures are shown to correlate with disease outcomes (Mathew et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Viral control and mild disease associate with the rapid generation of T-cells and antibodies targeting SARS-CoV-2.
source: Viral control and mild disease associate with the rapid generation of T-cells and antibodies targeting SARS-CoV-2 (Lucas et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2021), while severe disease is characterised by immune cell hyperactivation and a 'cytokine storm' (Chen et al., 2020; Kuri-Cervantes et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Severe disease is characterised by immune cell hyperactivation and a 'cytokine storm'.
source: Viral control and mild disease associate with the rapid generation of T-cells and antibodies targeting SARS-CoV-2 (Lucas et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2021), while severe disease is characterised by immune cell hyperactivation and a 'cytokine storm' (Chen et al., 2020; Kuri-Cervantes et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Commonly observed biomarkers of severe COVID-19 include lymphopenia, increased neutrophil to T-cell ratio, and elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines/mediators such as IL-6, IL-10, IL-17, MCP-1, IP-10, CRP, IL-1Rα, and IL-1β.
source: Commonly observed biomarkers of severe COVID-19 include lymphopenia, increased neutrophil to T-cell ratio, and elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines/mediators such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), IL-10, IL-17, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), interferon gamma-induced protein 10 (IP-10), CRP, IL-1Rα, and IL-1β.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about COVID-19 biomarkers.

claim: In a smaller proportion of individuals, severe COVID-19 may be driven by pre-existing anti-interferon gamma autoantibodies.
source: In a smaller proportion of individuals, severe COVID-19 may be driven by pre-existing anti-interferon gamma (anti-IFN-γ) autoantibodies (Bastard et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Lucas et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Distinctive features of severe disease include a dysregulation in the myeloid compartment consisting of increased circulating immature/dysfunctional neutrophils and immature Ki67+ COX-2low monocytes.
source: Other distinctive features of severe disease include a dysregulation in the myeloid compartment consisting of increased circulating immature/dysfunctional neutrophils and immature Ki67+ COX-2low monocytes (Mann et al., 2020; Schulte-Schrepping et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Mardi et al., 2021), while T-cell activation and proliferation appears to be heterogenous in severe patients (Mathew et al., 2020; Kuri-Cervantes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: T-cell activation and proliferation appears to be heterogenous in severe patients.
source: Other distinctive features of severe disease include a dysregulation in the myeloid compartment consisting of increased circulating immature/dysfunctional neutrophils and immature Ki67+ COX-2low monocytes (Mann et al., 2020; Schulte-Schrepping et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Mardi et al., 2021), while T-cell activation and proliferation appears to be heterogenous in severe patients (Mathew et al., 2020; Kuri-Cervantes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Longitudinal studies show that immune abnormalities and inflammation may persist after severe COVID-19, with highly activated myeloid cells, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and persistently activated T-cells detected 8–12 months after COVID-19.
source: Longitudinal studies show that immune abnormalities and inflammation may persist after severe COVID-19, with highly activated myeloid cells, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and persistently activated T-cells detected 8–12 months after COVID-19 (Bergamaschi et al., 2021; Phetsouphanh et al., 2022; Taeschler et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Long COVID is observed in 8–21% of individuals following mild to severe COVID-19.
source: Long COVID is observed in 8–21% of individuals following mild to severe COVID-19, although a higher prevalence of symptoms is reported in patients requiring ICU admission and/or mechanical ventilation (Alwan, 2021; Nalbandian et al., 2021; Ballering et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A higher prevalence of long COVID symptoms is reported in patients requiring ICU admission and/or mechanical ventilation.
source: Long COVID is observed in 8–21% of individuals following mild to severe COVID-19, although a higher prevalence of symptoms is reported in patients requiring ICU admission and/or mechanical ventilation (Alwan, 2021; Nalbandian et al., 2021; Ballering et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Several studies have reported a correlation between long COVID symptoms and a more rapid decline of SARS-CoV-2 memory CD8+ T-cells and lower levels of cytotoxic SARS-CoV-2 N-specific CD8+ T-cells.
source: Several studies have reported a correlation between long COVID symptoms and a variety of immune profiles including a more rapid decline of SARS-CoV-2 memory CD8+ T-cells and lower levels of cytotoxic SARS-CoV-2 N-specific CD8+ T-cells (Peluso et al., 2021), increased levels of cytotoxic CD8+ T-cells, and elevated plasma levels of type I cytokines, IL-1β and IL-6 (Shuwa et al., 2021; Schultheiß et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Long COVID has been correlated with increased levels of cytotoxic CD8+ T-cells, and elevated plasma levels of type I cytokines, IL-1β and IL-6.
source: Several studies have reported a correlation between long COVID symptoms and a variety of immune profiles including a more rapid decline of SARS-CoV-2 memory CD8+ T-cells and lower levels of cytotoxic SARS-CoV-2 N-specific CD8+ T-cells (Peluso et al., 2021), increased levels of cytotoxic CD8+ T-cells, and elevated plasma levels of type I cytokines, IL-1β and IL-6 (Shuwa et al., 2021; Schultheiß et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A longitudinal study conducted in 69 patients found long COVID to associate with an altered immune blood cell transcriptome which included significant changes in genes involved in cell cycle, but not with the phenotypic profiles of these cells.
source: Another longitudinal study conducted in 69 patients found long COVID to associate with an altered immune blood cell transcriptome which included significant changes in genes involved in cell cycle, but not with the phenotypic profiles of these cells (Ryan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A large UK cohort study (PHOSP-COVID) of hospitalised COVID-19 patients identified female sex, obesity, and invasive mechanical ventilation as factors associated with a lower likelihood of full recovery.
source: A large UK cohort study (PHOSP-COVID) of hospitalised COVID-19 patients identified female sex, obesity, and invasive mechanical ventilation as factors associated with a lower likelihood of full recovery, with an overall recovery rate of 28.9% at both 5 and 12 months across all disease severities (Evans et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The PHOSP-COVID study found an overall recovery rate of 28.9% at both 5 and 12 months across all disease severities.
source: A large UK cohort study (PHOSP-COVID) of hospitalised COVID-19 patients identified female sex, obesity, and invasive mechanical ventilation as factors associated with a lower likelihood of full recovery, with an overall recovery rate of 28.9% at both 5 and 12 months across all disease severities (Evans et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Other cohort studies have identified associations between poor recovery from COVID-19 and demographic factors such as sex and age.
source: Similarly, other cohort studies have identified associations between poor recovery from COVID-19 and demographic factors such as sex and age, but also highlight a possible role of immune dysregulation that occurs in older age, obesity and asthma, which warrants further investigation (Sneller et al., 2022; Halpin et al., 2021; Thompson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Hypotheses proposed to explain the mechanisms underlying long COVID include unresolved lung tissue damage, the persistence of SARS-CoV-2 infection, the reactivation of latent viruses such as CMV and Epstein-Barr virus and autoimmunity.
source: Other hypotheses proposed to explain the mechanisms underlying long COVID include unresolved lung tissue damage, the persistence of SARS-CoV-2 infection, the reactivation of latent viruses such as human cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Epstein-Barr virus and autoimmunity (Proal and VanElzakker, 2021; Gatto et al., 2022; Plüß et al., 2021; Zollner et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Studies suggest that COVID-19 vaccination may reduce the risk of developing long COVID.
source: Studies suggest that COVID-19 vaccination may reduce the risk of developing long COVID (Al-Aly et al., 2022; Notarte et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: At 3 months post admission, patients' blood lymphocyte and neutrophil counts, CRP, and albumin levels had normalised to levels that remained similar at 8 months.
source: Overall, at 3 months post admission patients' blood lymphocyte and neutrophil counts, CRP, and albumin levels - which were mostly perturbated during the acute illness - had normalised to levels that remained similar at 8 months, suggesting a resolution of the peak inflammatory events occurring during the acute illness (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The frequencies and absolute numbers of CD4+ T-cells were similar in patients across disease severities at 3 months.
source: The frequencies and absolute numbers of CD4+ T-cells were similar in patients across disease severities (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: An increased frequency of CD4+ T-cells expressing CXCR3 was observed in severe compared to moderate patients at 3 months.
source: However, we observed an increased frequency of CD4+ T-cells expressing the peripheral homing receptor CXCR3 in severe compared to moderate patients and an increased frequency of CD4+ T-cells co-expressing the proliferation/activation markers Ki67 and CD38 in severe compared to mild patients (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: An increased frequency of CD4+ T-cells co-expressing Ki67 and CD38 was observed in severe compared to mild patients at 3 months.
source: However, we observed an increased frequency of CD4+ T-cells expressing the peripheral homing receptor CXCR3 in severe compared to moderate patients and an increased frequency of CD4+ T-cells co-expressing the proliferation/activation markers Ki67 and CD38 in severe compared to mild patients (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The overall differentiation status of CD4+ T-cells was similar in mild, moderate, and severe patients at 3 months.
source: The overall differentiation status of CD4+ T-cells, defined by the coordinated expression of CCR7 and CD45RA, was similar in mild, moderate, and severe patients, with high proportions of naïve (CCR7+ CD45RA+) and T central memory cells (CCR7+ CD45RA-, TCM) followed by detectable levels of T effector memory cells (CCR7- CD45RA-, TEM) and low frequencies of T effector memory re-expressing RA cells (CCR7- CD45RA+, TEMRA) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The most abundant naïve and TCM CD4+ T-cell subsets contained significantly higher levels of cells co-expressing HLA-DR+ CD38+, HLA-DR+ Ki67+, CD38+ granzyme B+ in severe compared to moderate/mild patients at 3 months.
source: The most abundant naïve and TCM CD4+ T-cell subsets contained significantly higher levels of cells co-expressing markers of activation, proliferation, and cytotoxic potential (HLA-DR+ CD38+, HLA-DR+ Ki67+, CD38+ granzyme B+) in severe compared to moderate/mild patients (Figure 1F–K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F–K.

claim: Unsupervised analysis by UMAP and FlowSOM revealed the presence of 15 distinct clusters of CD4+ T-cells characterised by a unique, coordinated expression of the analysed markers.
source: An unsupervised analysis by UMAP and FlowSOM revealed the presence of 15 distinct clusters of cells characterised by a unique, coordinated expression of the analysed markers (Figure 1L), shown as mean fluorescence intensity in the heatmap (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1L and M.

claim: Significantly higher frequencies of CD4+ T-cell clusters expressing HLA-DR, CD38, and Ki67 (populations 8 and 13) were found in severe compared to moderate patients.
source: These analyses revealed significantly higher frequencies in severe compared to moderate patients of clusters of cells expressing HLA-DR, CD38, and Ki67 (populations 8 and 13) as well as of cells that express CCR7 but lack expression of all other markers analysed, and which resemble undifferentiated, resting CD4+ T-cells (population 2) (Figure 1N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: A CD4+ T-cell population expressing CCR7 but lacking expression of all other markers analysed, resembling undifferentiated, resting CD4+ T-cells (population 2), was significantly higher in severe compared to moderate patients.
source: These analyses revealed significantly higher frequencies in severe compared to moderate patients of clusters of cells expressing HLA-DR, CD38, and Ki67 (populations 8 and 13) as well as of cells that express CCR7 but lack expression of all other markers analysed, and which resemble undifferentiated, resting CD4+ T-cells (population 2) (Figure 1N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: Population 2 of CD4+ T-cells accounted for up to 60% of cells in severe patients.
source: The latter population accounted for a large proportion of CD4+ T-cells (up to 60% of cells in severe patients).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the FlowSOM analysis results.

claim: A CD4+ T-cell population characterised by low levels of expression of all markers analysed (population 1) is decreased in severe compared to moderate patients.
source: A population characterised by low levels of expression of all markers analysed is decreased in severe compared to moderate patients (population 1, Figure 1N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: The frequencies and absolute numbers of circulating CD8+ T-cells were comparable in patients across disease severities at 3 months.
source: Similarly, the analyses of CD8+ T-cells showed comparable frequencies and absolute numbers of circulating CD8+ T-cells in patients across disease severities and increased levels of CD8+ T-cells expressing markers of activation (HLADR+CD38+) in severe compared to moderate patients and cytotoxicity (granzyme B+) in severe compared to mild patients (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Increased levels of CD8+ T-cells expressing activation markers (HLADR+CD38+) were observed in severe compared to moderate patients at 3 months.
source: Similarly, the analyses of CD8+ T-cells showed comparable frequencies and absolute numbers of circulating CD8+ T-cells in patients across disease severities and increased levels of CD8+ T-cells expressing markers of activation (HLADR+CD38+) in severe compared to moderate patients and cytotoxicity (granzyme B+) in severe compared to mild patients (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Increased levels of CD8+ T-cells expressing granzyme B were observed in severe compared to mild patients at 3 months.
source: Similarly, the analyses of CD8+ T-cells showed comparable frequencies and absolute numbers of circulating CD8+ T-cells in patients across disease severities and increased levels of CD8+ T-cells expressing markers of activation (HLADR+CD38+) in severe compared to moderate patients and cytotoxicity (granzyme B+) in severe compared to mild patients (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The overall differentiation status of CD8+ T-cells was comparable in patients across disease severities with detectable frequencies of naïve, TCM, TEM, and TEMRA cells at 3 months.
source: The overall differentiation status of CD8+ T-cells was comparable in patients across disease severities with detectable frequencies of naïve, TCM, TEM, and TEMRA cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CD8+ T-cells expressing markers of activation and cytotoxicity (HLADR+ CD38+ and CD38+ granzyme B+) could be detected at higher frequencies within TCM, TEM, and TEMRA subsets in severe compared to moderate and/or mild patients at 3 months.
source: CD8+ T-cells expressing markers of activation and cytotoxicity (HLADR+ CD38+ and CD38+ granzyme B+) could be detected at higher frequencies within TCM, TEM, and TEMRA subsets in severe compared to moderate and/or mild patients (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F–I.

claim: Unsupervised analysis by UMAP and FlowSOM of CD8+ T-cells showed the presence of 15 clusters of cells expressing the analysed markers.
source: Unsupervised analysis by UMAP and FlowSOM of CD8+ T-cells showed the presence of 15 clusters of cells expressing the analysed markers (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2J and K.

claim: The frequencies of a cluster of CD8+ T-cells expressing high levels of granzyme B and CD45RA (cluster 3) were significantly increased in both severe and moderate compared to mild patients.
source: The frequencies of a cluster of CD8+ T-cells expressing high levels of granzyme B and CD45RA (cluster 3) were significantly increased in both severe and moderate compared to mild patients and represented up to 50% of all CD8+ T-cells in severe/moderate groups and up to 30% in mild group (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: CD8+ T-cell cluster 3 represented up to 50% of all CD8+ T-cells in severe/moderate groups and up to 30% in mild group.
source: The frequencies of a cluster of CD8+ T-cells expressing high levels of granzyme B and CD45RA (cluster 3) were significantly increased in both severe and moderate compared to mild patients and represented up to 50% of all CD8+ T-cells in severe/moderate groups and up to 30% in mild group (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: CD8+ T-cells expressing high levels of CCR7 and intermediate levels of granzyme B, CXCR3, and CD56 (cluster 12) were increased significantly in both mild and severe compared to moderate patients.
source: CD8+ T-cells expressing high levels of CCR7 and intermediate levels of granzyme B, CXCR3, and CD56 were increased significantly in both mild and severe compared to moderate patients (cluster 12).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the FlowSOM analysis results.

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell activation and proliferation decreased significantly from 3 to 12 months and activated/proliferating T-cells were largely absent at 12 months.
source: Analysis of the T-cell phenotypes in the same patients at 12 months showed that CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell activation and proliferation decreased significantly from 3 to 12 months and activated/proliferating T-cells were largely absent at 12 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a significant decrease of activated/proliferating CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells (Ki67+ CD38+, HLA-DR+ CD38+) from 3 to 12 months.
source: Analysis by manual gating showed a significant decrease of activated/proliferating CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells (Ki67+ CD38+, HLA-DR+ CD38+) and of CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells expressing the peripheral tissue-homing receptor CXCR3+ from 3 to 12 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C,G-J ).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C,G-J.

claim: There was a significant decrease of CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells expressing CXCR3+ from 3 to 12 months.
source: Analysis by manual gating showed a significant decrease of activated/proliferating CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells (Ki67+ CD38+, HLA-DR+ CD38+) and of CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells expressing the peripheral tissue-homing receptor CXCR3+ from 3 to 12 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C,G-J ).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C,G-J.

claim: Unsupervised analysis by UMAP revealed similar distribution of T-cell clusters in patients with mild, moderate, and severe disease at 12 months.
source: An unsupervised analysis by UMAP revealed similar distribution of T-cell clusters in patients with mild, moderate, and severe disease at 12 months, while major differences were observed between patients from the three groups at 3 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Major differences in T-cell cluster distribution were observed between patients from the three groups at 3 months.
source: An unsupervised analysis by UMAP revealed similar distribution of T-cell clusters in patients with mild, moderate, and severe disease at 12 months, while major differences were observed between patients from the three groups at 3 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claim: The ongoing T-cell activation observed at 3 months in patients with severe disease had recovered by 12 months post admission to levels similar to those observed in patients with mild and moderate disease.
source: Our data suggests that the ongoing T-cell activation observed at 3 months in patients with severe disease had recovered by 12 months post admission to levels similar to those observed in patients with mild and moderate disease.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the longitudinal data comparing 3 and 12 months.

claim: Analysis of expression of markers of activation/proliferation in NK CD56dim and CD56bright cells did not show evidence of ongoing NK cell activation at 3 months.
source: Analysis of expression of the same markers of activation/proliferation in NK CD56dim and CD56bright cells did not show evidence of ongoing NK cell activation and NK cells were similar in patients who recovered from mild, moderate, and severe disease (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-F.

claim: NK cells were similar in patients who recovered from mild, moderate, and severe disease at 3 months.
source: Analysis of expression of the same markers of activation/proliferation in NK CD56dim and CD56bright cells did not show evidence of ongoing NK cell activation and NK cells were similar in patients who recovered from mild, moderate, and severe disease (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-F.

claim: Analysis of the frequencies and expression of activation markers of classical, intermediate, and non-classical monocytes showed similar frequencies of these cells across the disease severities and lack of ongoing activation at 3 months.
source: Similarly, analysis of the frequencies and expression of activation markers (CD80, CD68) of classical (CD14+ CD16-), intermediate (CD14+CD16+), and non-classical (CD14-CD16+) monocytes showed similar frequencies of these cells across the disease severities and lack of ongoing activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G-K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G-K.

claim: Similar frequencies of unconventional TCR-γδ T-cells were detected in patients with mild, moderate, and severe disease at 3 months.
source: Similar frequencies of unconventional TCR-γδ T-cells were detected in patients with mild, moderate, and severe disease and these cells lacked expression of markers of activation/proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2L-N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2L-N.

claim: TCR-γδ T-cells lacked expression of markers of activation/proliferation at 3 months.
source: Similar frequencies of unconventional TCR-γδ T-cells were detected in patients with mild, moderate, and severe disease and these cells lacked expression of markers of activation/proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2L-N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2L-N.

claim: CD19+ B cells from severe patients showed an increase in the expression of the activation marker CD80 compared to patients with mild disease at 3 months.
source: In contrast, CD19+ B cells from severe patients showed an increase in the expression of the activation marker CD80 compared to patients with mild disease, although expression of other markers of activation/proliferation did not differ (HLA-DR, CD38, and Ki67) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2O-R).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2O-R.

claim: Expression of other B cell markers of activation/proliferation (HLA-DR, CD38, and Ki67) did not differ between disease severities at 3 months.
source: In contrast, CD19+ B cells from severe patients showed an increase in the expression of the activation marker CD80 compared to patients with mild disease, although expression of other markers of activation/proliferation did not differ (HLA-DR, CD38, and Ki67) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2O-R).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2O-R.

claim: At 3 months the levels of IL-4, IL-7, IL-17, and TNF-α were significantly increased in the plasma of patients with severe compared to mild and/or moderate disease.
source: Our results show that at 3 months the levels of IL-4, IL-7, IL-17, and TNF-α were significantly increased in the plasma of patients with severe compared to mild and/or moderate disease, while IFN-γ was increased in moderate compared to mild patients.
evidence: This is supported by Luminex data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IFN-γ was increased in moderate compared to mild patients at 3 months.
source: Our results show that at 3 months the levels of IL-4, IL-7, IL-17, and TNF-α were significantly increased in the plasma of patients with severe compared to mild and/or moderate disease, while IFN-γ was increased in moderate compared to mild patients.
evidence: This is supported by Luminex data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IFN-γ was largely undetectable in the plasma of severe patients at 3 months.
source: Interestingly, IFN-γ was largely undetectable in the plasma of severe patients (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by Luminex data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A trend for increased levels of IL-18 was observed in the plasma of severe compared to mild and moderate patients but the difference was not significantly different at 3 months.
source: A trend for increased levels of IL-18 was observed in the plasma of severe compared to mild and moderate patients but the difference was not significantly different.
evidence: This is based on Luminex data analysis.

claim: There was a statistically significant decrease of plasma levels of IL-4, IL-12, IL-13, and TNF-α from 3 to 8 and/or 12 months.
source: We next investigated the kinetics of expression of these cytokines in patients at 3, 8, and 12 months post admission and observed a statistically significant decrease of plasma levels of IL-4, IL-12, IL-13, and TNF-α from 3 to 8 and/or 12 months, suggesting that at 3 months the levels of these cytokines may still be affected by events occurring during the acute phase of infection.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal Luminex data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: At 3 months the levels of IL-4, IL-12, IL-13, and TNF-α may still be affected by events occurring during the acute phase of infection.
source: We next investigated the kinetics of expression of these cytokines in patients at 3, 8, and 12 months post admission and observed a statistically significant decrease of plasma levels of IL-4, IL-12, IL-13, and TNF-α from 3 to 8 and/or 12 months, suggesting that at 3 months the levels of these cytokines may still be affected by events occurring during the acute phase of infection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the longitudinal cytokine data.

claim: IL-15 levels were similar at 3 and 8 months and decreased thereafter.
source: IL-15 levels were similar at 3 and 8 months and decreased thereafter (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal Luminex data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: IL-17 levels were higher at 3 months and progressively diminished over time, although differences were not statistically significant.
source: IL-17 levels were higher at 3 months and progressively diminished over time, although differences were not statistically significant.
evidence: This is based on longitudinal Luminex data analysis.

claim: IP-10 levels were higher at 8 and 12 months compared to 3 months.
source: In contrast, IP-10 levels were higher at 8 and 12 months compared to 3 months.
evidence: This is based on longitudinal Luminex data analysis.

claim: The plasma levels of IL-7, IFN-γ, IL-18, and MCP-1 were comparable at 3–12 months post admission.
source: The plasma levels of the other cytokines analysed including IL-7, IFN-γ, IL-18, and MCP-1 were comparable at 3–12 months post admission.
evidence: This is based on longitudinal Luminex data analysis.

claim: Co-culture of plasma from severe patients at 3 months induced upregulation of the IL-15Rα-chain on T-cells from healthy donors.
source: We observed a significant upregulation of the IL-15Rα-chain, the IL-15R subunit that binds directly to IL-15, in T-cells co-cultured in the presence of plasma from severe patients at 3 months compared to healthy donors (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by co-culture experiment data shown in Figure 3D and E.
